newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico petrochemical industry seen as tough sale.
newsitem.headline: Mexico petrochemical industry seen as tough sale.

text.p: Mexico's rush of privatizations scheduled for 1997 should proceed smoothly and draw a tidy sum for the government, although the petrochemical industry will be a hard sell, economists said Friday.

Next year Mexico is hoping to place on the auction block operating rights to the remaining railroads and ports, airports, satellites, radio spectrum, natural gas distribution rights and stakes in 61 petrochemical plants.
While economists told Reuters the assets are seen as extremely attractive, restrictions in the once-coveted petrochemical industry have laid a damper on company's investment plans.
The government decided amid anti-privatization pressure to allow only a minority stake in existing plants and full ownership of new ones.

Once considered likely bidders for the plants, companies such as conglomerates Grupo Alfa and Desc Sociedad de Fomento Industrial, have cautiously said they do not want to be minority partners with state-owned oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex), analysts said.

"These companies have said that if they make the investment, they want to bring in their own CEO, they want the ability to manage as they deem appropriate," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Although companies can build their own petrochemical plants, still using Pemex supplies, the cost of constructing an independent complex will often be unprofitable, economists said.

"The worst thing that can happen for an investor is for things not to be clear. The petrochemical sale all depends on the clarity of how the sector will be disincorporated," said an economist who asked to remain unnamed.
With the entry of new companies in the other privatizations, however, economists expect lower prices and greater efficiency.

"It has all the ingredients for taking the government out of the economic process, reducing the role of the Mexican government as a direct actor in the industry. It means more new partners for investment, a lower deficit and greater social spending," said Abel Beltran-del-Rio, director of Ciemex-Wefa consulting group.

Zedillo's expected $14 billion from privatizations appears achievable, economists agreed. They clashed, however, on whether the government will use the windfall to fund social development programs, pay back government debt or reduce the debt.
Economists cited recent competitive privatizations as evidence that Mexican assets will be in demand in 1997.

The 50-year operating concession of key Mexico-U.S. rail route, known as the Northeast Railway, was recently granted to a partnership between Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) and Kansas City Southern Industries Inc..
Although the companies' $1.4 billion bid for the route was considered excessive by many brokerages, they said the competitive bidding proved that buyers find Mexico attractive.
In bringing out-dated infrastructure into the modern age, companies are expected to invest in improvements, develop synergies with U.S. partners and slash traditionally excessive payrolls.

As a consequence, Mexico's unions have been the loudest opponents of the government's privatization scheme, begun in the previous administration and continued ploddingly under President Ernesto Zedillo.

"International experience indicates that in the first year (after a privatization) employment falls, then returns to previous levels with more skilled people," Isaac Katz, economics chair of Mexico's Autonomous Technical Institute, told Reuters.
He said improvements needed on the Northeast Railway track, for example, may require a boosted labor force in initial years.
Political factors could be another roadblock to 1997 privatizations, as mid-term elections could stir up nationalist, anti-privatization sentiment, economists said.
